https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62.text: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports By Steve Rosenberg Russia editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow and Dmitrov Published 17 September 2026 The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing). That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises. This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin. Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair. But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say. "We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently. That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story? Far from it. For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election. Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war. I said no surprises. But there have been some. "Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV. The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns. "The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me." In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch: "The Communist Party, onwards we go! "We're with the people, don't you know?" More X Factor than exit poll. Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly: "Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!" It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war. Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine "All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament. "In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma." I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others â like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine. And if a party doesn't support the war? One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters. Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election. "The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place. "It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred." Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat. "Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel." Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism. The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down. Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election. In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine. The war is front and centre of people's minds here. Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation" "We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen." "I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you." Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing. "What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are." Expectations are low that this election will change much. "Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied. "Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is." Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney (left) listens to Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as they arrive for a press conference at Parliament House in Canberra in March. Photo / David Gray, AFP It’s easy to love Europe, at least as a tourist. Sure, it’s expensive, but where isn’t on the Kiwi peso? Last year, my family and I had one of our best holidays ever in France: baguettes, bordeaux, Monet and Manet. History and civilisation are everywhere. Soon enough, we’d love to do Italy. Back in New Zealand, when I need escapism, I search European property sites. It’s tantalising how cheap a Provencal chateau or Italian villa can be, and these days it’s just one flight to the European Union from Australasia (admittedly from Perth on Qantas, but don’t get bogged down in details). This came to mind recently when EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen got cosy with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at her 2026 state of the union address over Canada becoming an “associate member” of the European Union. If it’s good enough for them, why not us Kiwis? Von der Leyen said she wanted to work with Carney “on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU”. Carney is keen too, with officials saying both sides want the closest possible relationship short of full membership. Why? Carney is certainly punching above his weight internationally. His Davos speech early this year, urging middle powers to build new coalitions as the superpowers become less reliable, drew widespread attention and praise. Since then, his stature has only grown, particularly among anti-Donald Trump types. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. With this EU bid, Carney and von der Leyen are pushing back against fractured geopolitics, protectionism and tariffs, and a world where might increasingly makes right. They say they aren’t creating a new great-power rival “only with better manners”, but clearly want to defend the rules-based system, shared values and democracy. Possible areas of co-operation include critical minerals, energy, tech, artificial intelligence (AI) and social media rules, climate, Ukraine, defence and economic security – possibly the kitchen sink too. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola later confirmed that, after Canada, Australia and New Zealand could also become associate members. Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has left the door open, echoing Carney’s call for middle powers to build coalitions in a UN General Assembly speech days ago. Our leaders appear silent. In fairness, associate membership does not formally exist and no one has done the work needed to define it. EU member states, many Canadian observers and officialdom down our way also seemed surprised by the von der Leyen-Carney love-in. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. But if Canada became an associate member – and Carney clearly wants to explore it – would it make sense for us to follow? The arguments are economic, co-operative and ultimately cultural. We already have a high-quality free trade agreement, while Canada’s is not fully ratified and Australia’s is not in force. In just over two years, Trade Minister Todd McClay says ours delivered more than $3 billion in additional exports, taking total exports to $8.8b in the year to December 2025. Greater connection and integration could lift that further in an exceptionally wealthy continent and the world’s second-largest economy by nominal gross domestic product (GDP). There is plenty of room to grow. There is a lively debate among financial leaders over Europe’s economic strength. JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon says its GDP relative to America’s keeps falling and calls it a high-tax, high-debt, anti-business place. Financial journalist Martin Wolf offers a persuasive rebuttal: the US and China lead in advanced digital technologies, but the EU still outperforms on measures such as life expectancy and, by some GDP measures, remains ahead. The easy caricature can mislead. On co-operation, Carney has cited a larger Canadian role in Horizon Europe, the EU’s huge research and innovation programme, the Erasmus student exchange and more youth work exchanges. New Zealand already benefits as one of the first non-European participants in Horizon Europe – before Canada and Australia – and could gain from similar people-to-people ties. An agreement might also bring greater EU involvement in our Pacific or Antarctic responsibilities, which could really help. But the people-to-people and cultural possibilities may be most exciting. My wife is half Polish; Poland has grown strongly since joining the EU, moving from David Lange’s pejorative “Polish shipyard” status to the world’s 20th-largest economy. We met at university in the UK when it was in the EU. Wouldn’t we want more young Europeans coming here to study, work, meet someone and perhaps settle? Politically incorrect though it may sound, history, culture, shared values and democratic tradition give us more in common with the EU than most. That is worth nurturing. The case against is also clear. We already have an excellent free trade agreement: would squeezing the lemon harder produce much more juice? Greater integration would mean more regulatory alignment and Europe is hardly light-touch on red tape. David Seymour and his Ministry for (or against) Regulation would not approve. Co-operation could also bring greater obligations on, say, defence and security, for example, in Ukraine. We already assist, but more might be required. We are also a long way from Europe. Some tell me this thinking is very 19th century: we can get there in a day and values now matter more than geography. Yet distance has produced differences. We are a Pacific nation, with Polynesian and European whakapapa, and increasingly Asian in demography and outlook. I love visiting Europe but professionally, the Asia-Pacific – or Indo-Pacific, as it is now fashionable to say – is where it’s at and where I spend more time. Then there is Trump, who called the associate-member idea “a hostile act” and threatened higher tariffs. Would two of our biggest economic partners — the United States and China, also the world’s superpowers – object? Could it upset the apple, or kiwifruit, cart? It might. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. I love Europe, but we should watch and learn from Canada’s first-mover effort. Nothing will happen for us or Australia unless Canada succeeds. Until then, we can sit in its slipstream like those skinny Europeans pedalling behind the Tour de France leader: let Canada make the effort while we cruise close behind. That makes sense. Associate membership is untested and would be hard work: all 27 EU states would need to agree. But Carney is right. In this uncertain age, middle powers must keep building coalitions. And the baguettes and bordeaux are wonderful. Catch up on the debates that dominated the week by signing up to our Opinion newsletter – a weekly round-up of our best commentary.
